newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - BMW profits reinforce rosy outlook.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BMW profits reinforce rosy outlook.

text.p: German luxury carmaker Bayerische Motoren Werke (BMW) said on Thursday net profit climbed 18.5 percent last year to 820 million marks ($486.4 million) after hot-selling new models boosted sales to a record high.

The profit figures, in line with analysts' forecasts, reinforced expectations that BMW would post higher profits and sales growth in 1997, despite questions surrounding the future of its mainstay 3-Series model.
"Its a reasonably confident picture for BMW going forward," said John Lawson, car analyst at Salomon Brothers. "Profits will be higher in 1997."

In a brief statement on its results, BMW said it would increase its dividend to 15 marks per share from 13.50 marks a year ago and that group profit from ordinary activities climbed to 1.66 billion marks from 1.37 billion marks.
The company will hold its annual press conference next Tuesday when it will offer a first view of its expectations for 1997 and provide a break down of the 1996 results.
Analysts attributed the profit growth to three factors -- healthy demand for two recently introduced models, a stronger dollar and probably a smaller loss at BMW's British unit, Rover Group.

BMW announced in January that group sales last year climbed more than 13 percent to a record 52.27 billion marks, largely on the back of its latest 5-Series executive class saloon and the Z3 two-seat roadster which is made in the U.S.

Foreign exchange markets are also thought to have helped BMW which had suffered under a strong mark last year. The dollar's steady climb to 31-month highs last year increases the number of marks the BMW makes for sales in the U.S.
Although Rover's financial results have not been released, analysts said the unit will likely report a smaller loss in 1996 than last year's 335 million mark shortfall.
Greater efficiencies thanks to BMW investment and higher sales should help the unit break even as BMW expects around 2000, analysts said.
"All in all, the figures look about as expected," said Georg Stuerzer, car analyst at Vereinsbank Research in Munich. "Profit is coming from BMW's core business."

BMW, however, is notorious for its conservative accounting practices and analysts said they will closely watch next Tuesday's press conference for how BMW arrived at the profit figure, paying close attention to DVFA earnings per share.
"Only next week will we be able to see how much BMW has added back for provisions," an analyst said. "It will be a much better indicator of the quality of the company's results."
Analysts figure BMW should be able to report a net profit of around 950 million marks for 1997, but add that a couple question marks hang over the company.
First, the hugely popular 3-Series model is soon due for a new edition after being introduced 1991.
BMW is keeping mum about when the new car will come out, but analysts figure slowing demand for the model will become more pronounced when Munich officially announces the new car.
Car buyers tend not to buy a particular model in its final year of production, preferring to wait until they can buy the latest edition.
Second, Rover, is expected to have a difficult time maintaining sales growth this year with its new Land Rover model not hitting the market until late in the year.
A source close to Rover said in February that 1996 sales should be around 16 billion marks, up from 13 billion marks reported in 1995.
"Rover could see sales stagnate or even slip a bit in 1997," the auto industry analyst said.
($ = 1.686 German Marks)
